name: Quit India movement
info: The Quit India movement was a mass campaign launched by Mahatma Gandhi and the All India Congress Committee on 8 August 1942, during the Second World War, demanding an end to British rule in India; it ended in 1945 with the release of jailed nationalists.

facts.where: British India, with the strongest local effects at Satara in Maharashtra, Talcher in Odisha, Midnapore in Bengal, Ballia in what is now Uttar Pradesh, parts of Saurashtra in Gujarat and, with the greatest violence, Bihar
facts.period: Congress working committee resolution at Wardha on 14 July 1942; launch at Bombay on 8 August 1942; mass arrests and local risings from August to September 1942; underground resistance and parallel governments, with leaders in prison, until 1945; release of all jailed nationalists in 1945
facts.figures: Mohandas Gandhi, who called on the people to Do or Die; Jawaharlal Nehru and Maulana Azad, who were apprehensive but backed the call; Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad, who supported it openly; Aruna Asaf Ali, who presided over the All India Congress Committee session on 9 August; Jayaprakash Narayan and Asoka Mehta; underground leaders such as Achyut Rao Patwardhan, Sucheta Kripalani and Nana Patil
facts.outcome: almost all of the Congress leadership was imprisoned, more than 100,000 people were arrested and hundreds of civilians were killed; the movement ended in 1945 with the release of the jailed nationalists, after Labour won the British election promising independence for India

t: Gandhi launched the movement in Bombay on 8 August 1942 with a call to Do or Die, after the Cripps Mission failed to win Indian support for the war effort, and almost the whole Congress leadership was in prison within hours.

Without its leaders the movement took the form of strikes, boycotts, sabotage and local parallel governments, and the British answered with more than 100,000 arrests, mass fines, public flogging and the killing of hundreds of civilians.
The Muslim League, the Hindu Mahasabha, the Communist Party of India and some princes opposed the movement, while Viceroy Linlithgow called it by far the most serious rebellion since 1857.
dyk: Viceroy Linlithgow told Winston Churchill in a telegram of 31 August 1942 that the gravity and extent of the rebellion had been concealed from the world for reasons of military security.
ev: India is brought into the war without consultation, and the Congress ministers of eight provinces resign
The Cripps Mission fails to win Congress support, and Gandhi calls its offer a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank
The Congress working committee at Wardha adopts a resolution demanding complete independence on 14 July
Gandhi delivers his Quit India speech at Bombay on 8 August, and almost the entire Congress leadership is imprisoned within hours
Between 9 August and 21 September protesters attack post offices, railway stations and police stations, and 57 battalions of British troops are deployed
Gandhi is released on account of his health and demands the release of the Congress leadership
All jailed nationalists are released after the Labour Party wins the British election

sections.background:
In 1939 Indian nationalists were angry that the Governor-General, Lord Linlithgow, brought India into the war without consulting them. India became a party to the war as a constituent part of the British Empire. The Muslim League supported the war, but Congress was divided. At Wardha in September 1939 the Congress working committee conditionally supported the fight against the Axis but was rebuffed when it asked for independence in return, and on 10 October it resolved that India could not associate herself with the war unless she was consulted first.

When the Viceroy answered on 17 October that the government would modify the Act of 1935 after the war, Gandhi said that Congress had asked for bread and got stone. The Congress ministers of eight provinces resigned on the party's instructions. Muhammad Ali Jinnah called 22 December 1939, the day of the resignations, the Day of Deliverance, and in March 1940 declared at the Muslim League's Lahore session that the Muslims wanted a separate electorate, Pakistan. In August the Viceroy issued the "August Offer", which Congress rejected, followed by the Muslim League.

Gandhi then began individual civil disobedience, with Vinoba Bhave chosen to open it; almost fourteen thousand satyagrahis were arrested, and the Viceroy ordered their acquittal on 3 December 1941. After the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor the movement was withdrawn.
sections.aims:
The Cripps Mission of March 1942 was sent to win total co-operation during the war in return for devolution of power to an elected Indian legislature. Its draft declaration promised a dominion and a Constituent Assembly, but only after the war, and it set out no timetable of self-government or of the powers to be relinquished. Congress saw an offer of limited dominion status and a promise for the future; Gandhi called it "a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank". The threat of Japanese invasion and the leaders' conviction that the British could not defend India also weighed on the decision.

The Congress working committee at Wardha on 14 July 1942 adopted a resolution demanding complete independence and sanctioning "a mass struggle on non-violent lines on the widest possible scale", adding that "non-violence is the basis of the movement". It was passed at Bombay. Gandhi spoke of "An Orderly British Withdrawal", and his speech of 8 August at the Gowalia Tank Maidan called on the people to Do or Die.

The guidelines included disobedience of law, general strikes among students and labour, the formation of free government, breaking communications and refusing to pay taxes. On 8 November 1942 Congress told people to perform ten duties "without any risk", among them to have no business with the British or their government, to show the tricoloured flag at every home and window, to stay out of the courts, to withdraw money from government banks, to leave the cities for the villages and to let the grain remain with the peasant.
sections.events:
Within hours of Gandhi's speech on 8 August 1942 almost the entire Congress leadership was imprisoned without trial, and most of them spent the rest of the war in prison and out of contact with the masses. Because of the arrests Aruna Asaf Ali, then relatively unknown, presided over the All India Congress Committee session on 9 August and hoisted the flag; the Congress party was later banned. Workers stayed away in large groups, strikes were called and demonstrations were held across the country, some of which turned violent, with bombs, burning buildings and severed transport and communications.

According to John F. Riddick, from 9 August to 21 September 1942 the movement attacked 550 post offices and 250 railway stations, destroyed 70 police stations and burned or damaged 85 other government buildings. The greatest violence occurred in Bihar, and the government deployed 57 battalions of British troops. On 31 August Linlithgow described "by far the most serious rebellion since that of 1857" to Churchill.

Without national leadership the effect was local. At Tamluk and Contai in Midnapore the people set up the Tamluk National Government, which lasted until Gandhi asked its leaders to disband in 1944. At Ballia people overthrew the district administration, broke open the jail and freed the Congress leaders, and it took weeks to restore British authority. At Adas village in Kaira district six people died in a police shooting. In rural west Bengal peasants resented war taxes and forced rice exports until the great famine of 1943 suspended the movement there.
sections.people:
Gandhi had not supported Congress's initiative of 1939, because he could not reconcile it with his belief in non-violent resistance. Within Congress the call for 1942 proved controversial. Chakravarti Rajagopalachari quit the party over it, as did some local and regional organisers. Jawaharlal Nehru and Maulana Azad were apprehensive and critical but backed it and stayed with Gandhi's leadership. Vallabhbhai Patel, Rajendra Prasad and Anugrah Narayan Sinha supported it openly, as did Asoka Mehta, Jayaprakash Narayan and many veteran Gandhians and socialists.

Allama Mashriqi of the Khaksar Tehrik, whom Nehru invited to join, telegraphed Azad, Gandhi, Nehru and others on 28 July that civil disobedience was "a little pre-mature" and that Congress should first concede "the theoretical Pakistan" to the Muslim League. Aruna Asaf Ali, Achyut Rao Patwardhan, Sucheta Kripalani, Daljit Singh and Nana Patil led the underground movement, which used clandestine radio stations, pamphlets and parallel governments. Mukunda Kakati, Matangini Hazra, Kanaklata Barua, Kushal Konwar and Bhogeswari Phukanani were among the activists who died during the movement.

Subash Chandra Bose, who had organised the Indian Legion in Germany and reorganised the Indian National Army with Japanese help, said that a new chapter in the freedom struggle began with the movement.
sections.outcomes:
The British responded swiftly with mass detentions. More than 100,000 arrests were made, mass fines were levied and demonstrators were publicly flogged. Hundreds of civilians were killed, many of them shot. The sense of crisis was strong enough that a battleship was set aside to take Gandhi and the Congress leaders out of India, possibly to South Africa or Yemen, but the step was not taken for fear of intensifying the revolt. The movement also pulled British forces away from the war: 57 infantry battalions were used to quell protests for months, and airfield construction was delayed by four to six weeks.

The Congress leadership was cut off from the world for over three years. Gandhi's wife Kasturba Gandhi and his secretary Mahadev Desai died within months, and his health was failing, but he went on a 21-day fast. He was released in 1944 on account of his health and kept up his demand for the release of the Congress leadership.

Opponents gained from the situation. The Muslim League under Jinnah, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and the Hindu Mahasabha sought political mileage and criticised Gandhi and Congress, and a sense that the movement could not bring prompt results depressed many nationalists. The movement did keep Congress united through these trials. In 1945, as the war was nearly over, the Labour Party won the British election with a promise of Indian independence, and the jailed prisoners were released.
sections.legacy:
Ultimately the British realised that India was ungovernable in the long run, and the question for the postwar era became how to leave gracefully and peacefully. The movement ended in 1945 with the release of all jailed nationalists.

The opposition to it shaped later argument. The Hindu Mahasabha officially boycotted the movement, and its president Vinayak Damodar Savarkar wrote a letter, Stick to your Posts, telling Hindu Sabhaites who were members of municipalities, local bodies, legislatures or the army not to join it; later, after requests and persuasion, he chose to join the independence movement. On 26 July 1942 Syama Prasad Mukherjee, the Mahasabha's leader in Bengal and a minister in Fazlul Haq's coalition government, wrote to the Governor that anyone planning to stir up mass feeling during the war must be resisted by any government in office, and that the movement should be made to fail to take root in Bengal. The Muslim League and Jinnah supported the British war effort. The Communist Party of India opposed the movement and supported the war after the Soviet Union was attacked, and some princes opposed it and funded the opposition. The major outside support came from the Americans, as President Roosevelt pressured Churchill to give in to some of the Indian demands; after Churchill threatened to resign if pushed too hard, the United States quietly supported him.

In 1992 the Reserve Bank of India issued a one rupee commemorative coin for the Golden Jubilee of the movement.

summary: The Quit India movement was a mass campaign launched by Gandhi at Bombay on 8 August 1942 demanding an end to British rule. Its leaders were jailed within hours; strikes, sabotage and local governments followed, and the British made over 100,000 arrests. It ended in 1945 with the release of jailed nationalists.
references: D. N. Panigrahi, India's Partition: The Story of Imperialism in Retreat (Routledge, 2004)
Pran Nath Chopra, Quit India Movement: British secret documents, Vol. 1 (Interprint, 1986)
notes: Dates: the lede says the movement ended in 1945 with the release of all jailed nationalists; used as end. The release is given only as 1945.
The article gives Gandhi's 8 August speech and the working committee's Wardha meeting of 14 July 1942; it says the resolution 'was passed at Bombay' without a date.
The August Offer is dated '8 August' in the article with no year (placed after Churchill replaced Chamberlain); I wrote 'In August' with no year.

Left out: the article's claim that Syama Prasad Mukherjee 'managed to gain insights of the British government and effectively give information of the independence leaders' (an unsourced assertion in a contested political context). Mukherjee's letter is reported as written.
Left out: the article's statement that 'many shot by the police army' is ungrammatical; written 'many of them shot'.
The article gives the date of Gandhi's 21-day fast and the death of Kasturba Gandhi and Mahadev Desai only as 'in months'; the release of Gandhi 'in 1944'. Kept as given.
Bose is spelt 'Subash' as in the article.
The ten duties are dated 8 November 1942 in the article; a selection of them is given.
